messages.subject: combining centered & non-centered params
parts:
[moved to stan-dev]

Backstory: we're evaluating IRT models in Stan vs. Stata and
Daniel Furr (at Berkeley, working with Sophia Rabe-Hesketh) switched
the parameterization from centered to non-centered at Andrew's behest
and found sampling slowed down by a factor of four or so (see below
for details). Andrew wanted to stick with non-centered as our
recommended parameterization even in this example. But that's not
what this mail's about, it's about the follow on.

Andrew's been talking about combining centered and non-centered parameterizations
in a single model. I recall something like that in a paper by XL et al. for
Metropolis or Gibbs.

What I don't understand is how you would "switch back and forth between them"
if you compiled them separately. They have different parameters.

Now I could imagine something that looked like this:

alpha[n] <- (1 - lambda) * gamma + beta[jj[n]]

where

beta ~ normal(lambda * gamma, sigma);

lambda ~ uniform(0, 1);

So lambda would control how much centering (lambda = 0 is non-centered,
lambda = 1 is centered). I think the likelihood is the same for all
lambda in [0, 1], so we'd need some way to prefer the one that works
more efficiently. Which seems like something we have to do outside
the Stan language.

- Bob

> On Oct 1, 2015, at 7:09 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

But I agree that this is off-topic for this discussion.
>
> It was my understanding that stan_lme (or whatever it’s now called) automatically uses the noncentered parameterization so I think of it as our default.
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] combining centered & non-centered params
parts:
One is free to use a centered or non-centered parameterization
for each _group_, but within a group that choice must be consistent.
This gets even uglier when you have hierarchical models with many
layers — if you think about the hierarchical model as a tree then you
can choose between the two parameterizations at every node. Using
both parameterizations for different groups is straightforward, if a bit
ungainly.

Now if you’re talking about switching between the parameterizations
after Markov transitions then everything becomes significantly more
complicated. The problem is that centered and non-centered
parameterizations aren’t really parameterizations — they’re identifying
different target spaces all together. In other words, they require
different parameter blocks.

Say beta is the centered parameter,

beta ~ normal(mu, sigma),

and beta_tilde is the non-centered parameter,

beta_tilde ~ normal(0, 1),
beta = mu + sigma * beta_tilde.

In order to interleave transitions using each you’d have to do something
like

transition_using_beta
...
transition_using_beta_tilde
beta = mu + sigma * beta_tilde
…
transition_using_beta
...

And so on. In Stan this would essentially reduce to switching between
parameters and transformed parameters and a giant rabbit hole of how
to identify what to switch and how to switch. And all of that assumes
that we can even identify what groups should be in what parameterization,
which is beyond our current capabilities — we can identify when at least
one group is poorly parameterized, but which group.

So, um, good luck?

Thanks for clarifying. It's what I was fumbling toward
with "different parameters".

If we consider transformed params, they have the same
posteriors. But they sample over different subsets of them.
But those subsets are easily transformed back and forth.

So I don't see any reason why we couldn't jump back and
forth in some kind of specialized MCMC that randomized
which stepper to use. Or does that not define a proper Markov
chain? I don't see why not. It's all kinds of crazy w.r.t.
HMC because it's a lower dimensional given the deterministic
relationship between some of the "parameters".

- Bob

Hi, I have 2 thoughts:

1. In a program such as stan_lme which must set up the model automatically, we could have 2 models, one where all variance components have the centered paraemterization, the other where all variance components have the noncentered parameterization. And Stan could alternate between these. This might be a safer option than just doing one or the other. (If we just do one, it’s my impression that the noncentered parameterization is safer in that things can sometimes go really really wrong with the centered parameterization.)

2. What about a model that includes both as special cases, for example:

theta ~ normal(0,sigma_theta);
for (n in 1:N)

y_pred[n] <- mu + tau_theta*theta[group[n]];
y ~ normal(y_pred, sigma_y);

In this case, if you set sigma_theta <- 1 you get the noncentered parameterization and if you set tau_theta <- 1 you get the centered parameterization. So one option would be to put some pseudo-prior on sigma_theta and sigma_tau, something that could allow the best of both in that it could allow the HMC to “find” the smoother regions of space.

Could this work?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] combining centered & non-centered params
parts:
On Friday, October 2, 2015 at 10:57:24 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
1.  In a program such as stan_lme which must set up the model automatically, we could have 2 models, one where all variance components have the centered paraemterization, the other where all variance components have the noncentered parameterization.  And Stan could alternate between these.  This might be a safer option than just doing one or the other.

In principle, we could have flags for different parameterizations but in practice that would be a difficult rabbit hole for the code to go down. Also, it is inconsistent with the principle that we have adhered to thusfar: stan_foo() does not reparameterize foo(). Since [g]lmer does a Matt-trick parameterization of the linear predictor where

eta = X * beta + Z * b
b = sigma * L * z
z ~ normal(0,1)
Sigma = sigma^2 * L * L'

that is what we have done with stan_glmer, which also allows use to use lme4's formula parser to ensure that we are faithfully representing the likelihood (which was the hurdle we couldn't get over with glmer2stan and Rayleigh's stuff) and doing the posterior predictive distribution right. Finally, we have not conceived of the target audience for rstanarm as being sufficiently well-versed in this stuff to make a choice like this. By default, they don't even see any measure of the efficiency of the sampler.
(If we just do one, it’s my impression that the noncentered parameterization is safer in that things can sometimes go really really wrong with the centered parameterization.)

I am going to hope that things will only rarely go really really wrong with our prior on (the decomposition of) Sigma.

Ben

parts:
Notation: non-centering refers to both the location and the scale.  Think
of it as a total non-centering in both linear space (location) and log space (scale).

In fact the location non-centering gets complicated by the non-identifiabiltiy of
means in a multilevel model.  Once you fit to a single common mean the scale
is usually the only thing left to shift anyways.

Performance: the two parameterization performances are symmetry.  With sparse
data the non-centered parameterization is better, with dense data the centered
parameterization is better.  Assuming that we’re using a hierarchical model
because there’s not enough data to fit everything independently, the non-centered 
is a reasonable default.

I always default to a non-centered but I do keep coming across examples where
there’s just enough data to make the separation between the two parameterizations
more ambiguous.
